title: Pain Masking in Prey Companion Animals: Integrating PAG-RVM Descending Modulation with Antipredator Evolutionary Theory
content: Prey companion species — rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas, and small rodents — are clinically recognized for concealing overt signs of pain, a behavior long attributed loosely to "prey instinct." This review proposes an integrated neuroanatomical-evolutionary framework explaining why and how this masking occurs. We synthesize evidence on the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), the core descending pain-modulation circuit, and link its function to stress-induced analgesia (SIA), a conserved antipredator adaptation that suppresses nociceptive output during acute threat exposure. We argue that pain masking is not a passive absence of expression but an active, centrally mediated suppression mechanism with clear survival value: an animal displaying pain is a visible target for predators. We map documented behavioral pain indicators (grimace scales, postural changes, activity suppression) onto this circuit-level mechanism and discuss the direct clinical consequence — systematic underestimation of pain severity — with implications for analgesic protocol design in exotic companion medicine. We conclude with testable predictions, such as context-dependent grimace-scale variability under simulated predator cues, that could validate the framework experimentally. This synthesis aims to shift the clinical narrative from "hard to read" prey species toward a mechanistically grounded model that can inform pain-assessment tools and analgesic dosing philosophy in rabbits, rodents, and other small exotic mammals.
